strings.step.overview.title: Posterior Cervical Foraminotomy (PCF)
strings.step.overview.body:
Posterior cervical foraminotomy (PCF) is a surgical procedure that relieves pressure on the spinal cord and nerves by **widening the neural foramen posteriorly**.
A major advantage of PCF is that it allows patients to **preserve range of motion** after the surgery.
During the procedure, surgeons may additionally perform **discectomy** or **osteophytectomy** to achieve adequate decompression and symptom relief.

strings.step.indications.title: Indication for PCF
strings.step.indications.body:
PCF is commonly performed to treat conditions that affect spinal nerves as they exit the **neural foramen**.
Examples of conditions where PCF may be considered are:
- **Cervical spondylotic radiculopathy**
- **Lateral cervical disc herniation**
- **Foraminal stenosis**
In this 3D model, a C4-C5 intervertebral disc is herniated **laterally**, compressing the spinal nerve as it exits through the neural foramen.
Such a condition can cause a variety of symptoms, such as numbness, tingling, and pain in the upper extremity.
In severe cases of herniation, the intervertebral disc may compress the spinal cord, affecting balance, walking, or sensory deficits of the lower extremities.

strings.step.laminoforaminotomy.title: Laminoforaminotomy
strings.step.laminoforaminotomy.body:
During PCF, surgeons first identify the precise location where the surgery will be performed using medical imaging and anatomical landmarks.
The surgeons then carefully remove parts of the bone near the neural foramen, a procedure known as **laminoforaminotomy**.
This creates more space around the nerve to escape from the pressing disc.
In some cases, creating this opening allows surgeons to **directly observe** the herniated disc.

strings.step.microdiscectomy.title: Microdiscectomy
strings.step.microdiscectomy.body:
When necessary, surgeons further perform a **discectomy** to ensure that the nerve is fully decompressed.
To perform this step safely and accurately, surgeons may use special types of **microscopes** during disc removal, a procedure known as **microdiscectomy**.
**Osteophytectomy** may additionally be considered if there is a clear visualization of the osteophyte.
strings.step.microdiscectomy.accessibility: Microdiscectomy. When necessary, surgeons further perform a **discectomy** to ensure that the nerve is fully decompressed.
strings.step.preserved_motion.title: Preserved Motion after PCF
strings.step.preserved_motion.body:
One of the advantages of performing PCF is that it allows patients to maintain **normal neck motion** after the surgery.
Unlike **[posterior cervical decompression and fusion (PCDF)](procedure:pcdf)** and **[anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF)](procedure:acdf)**, PCF does not require the spine to be fused permanently, owing to the minimally invasive nature of this procedure.
However, PCF may not be suitable for conditions that require surgical interventions on **multiple vertebral levels**.
Performing PCF on multiple levels may lead to **spinal instability**, which could in turn lead to worsening of symptoms.

strings.step.summary.title: Summary
strings.step.summary.body:
Some of the key features of PCF are as follows:
- It is a procedure where a small portion of bone is removed from the spine to create more space around the **neural foramen**.
- Surgeons may additionally perform a **discectomy** and **osteophytectomy** to ensure adequate pressure relief.
- It **preserves the range of motion** of the cervical spine but may not be suitable for **multilevel disorders**.
Due to its minimally invasive nature, PCF may be considered an alternative to fusion surgeries for selected patients with cervical compression.
